title: A job queue for worker threads
description:
Build `JobQueue`, a thread-safe queue of `int` jobs that worker threads can wait on.

- `push(job)` adds a job and wakes one waiting worker.
- `pop()` waits until a job is available and returns it. If the queue has been **closed** and is empty, it returns `std::nullopt` instead of waiting, so workers know to finish.
- `close()` marks the queue closed and wakes every waiting worker. Jobs already queued are still handed out.
- `tryPop()` returns a job if one is waiting, or `std::nullopt` immediately.

Use a `std::mutex` and a `std::condition_variable`. The tests start several worker threads.
hints: `std::deque<int>` (from `<deque>`) is a sequence that is cheap to change at both ends, which makes it a natural queue: `m_jobs.push_back(job)` adds at the back, `m_jobs.front()` reads the oldest job, `m_jobs.pop_front()` removes it, and `m_jobs.empty()` says whether any are left.

`std::optional<T>` (from `<optional>`) holds either a `T` or nothing. `return value;` gives back a filled one and `return std::nullopt;` an empty one. A caller tests it with `if (result)` (or `result.has_value()`) and reads the value inside with `*result`.
Every function that touches `m_jobs` or `m_closed` must hold `m_mutex`. `pop` needs a `std::unique_lock`, because `wait` has to unlock it while sleeping.
`m_ready.wait(lock, predicate)` sleeps until the predicate is true, checking it again after every wake-up. The condition to wait for is "there is a job, or the queue is closed".
`push` wakes one worker with `notify_one`; `close` must wake them all with `notify_all`, or idle workers would sleep forever.
